newsitem.title: USA: Oakland task force steers clear of Ebonics.
newsitem.headline: Oakland task force steers clear of Ebonics.

text.p: An Oakland schools task force that whipped up a storm over Ebonics or Black English did not mention the controversial subject in its final report released Tuesday.

The Task Force on the Education of African-American Students presented a proposed five-year plan to improve educational opportunities for the Oakland School District's black students, who make up 53 percent of total enrollment.
The 23-page report contained no reference to Ebonics, a form of speech used by inner-city blacks.
The Oakland school board was acting on the task force's recommendations in December 1996 when it adopted a policy recognising Ebonics as a distinct language.
The ensuing outcry forced the school board to amend the policy in January, removing a reference to Ebonics as the "primary language" of many African-American students.

Some critics took the original policy to mean that the board wanted African-American students to be taught in Ebonics. Oakland school officials strongly denied that in January. By recognising Ebonics, they said they hoped to improve the way black students were taught to read and write standard English.
The task force's final report, which must be approved by the school board, calls for a comprehensive English-language development programme for African-American students.

It says a community coordinator should be hired to serve as a liaison between the school district, parents and the community. It calls for an aggressive recruitment plan to increase the number of black teachers and administrators in the district and emphasises training and staff development.
The plan calls for spending $2 million over five years.

"Our focus is, and has always been, on the development of long-range strategies to improve academic achievement for African-American students," task force Chairman Sylvester Hodges said in a statement.
Task force members denied at a news conference that they were shying away from the term "Ebonics", which is derived from "ebony" and "phonics."
